title: Politics is tearing my family apart
seoTitle: When Politics Divides Your Family: Faith and What Helps
description: When politics turns family dinners into fights: what Scripture says, how to talk and when to stop, and how to keep loving people who vote differently.
summary: When the fight at the table is about the flag or the cause: an older allegiance than either.
askedAs: my parents watch the news all day
can a Christian be a Democrat
can a Christian be a Republican
What does the Bible say about politics?
answer: You love them, and you can hardly be in the same room anymore. Maybe it's a father who has the news on from breakfast to bedtime, a grown daughter who treats you as part of what's wrong with the country, a brother you haven't called since the last election, or a holiday you're already dreading. Under the arguments is grief: you're losing someone who is still alive. You don't have to win them over, or agree with them, to keep loving them. This week, have one conversation with no politics in it, and in the next hard one, ask a question and listen before you answer. If an argument has turned into threats, or you're afraid of someone at home, that's a safety problem: call 911 if you're in danger now, or use the hotlines at the end of this page.
happening:
It might be Thanksgiving, or a family group text that goes quiet after someone posts a link. It might be a mother who hears every question as an attack, a son who came home with convictions that sound like an accusation, or a marriage where you've agreed not to talk about it because you know where it goes. The words that wound are usually short: *How can you vote for that?* *You've been brainwashed.* *I don't even know who you are anymore.* It hurts this much because you love them, and these are the faces you know best.

It hurts on both sides of the table. Parents fear their grown children have thrown away what they were raised to believe, and grown children wonder how the parents who taught them to love their neighbor can talk this way. In some families it's the other way around, and a son who moved right is the one his parents can't recognize. Each side is frightened, and each is sure the other is the danger. If you're a Christian, you may also hear your own faith used against you.

The usual explanations each hold part of the truth. The news and the feeds are built to hold attention, and fear and anger hold it well, so a parent who watches for hours, or a teenager who scrolls for hours, hears all day that the other side is coming for what they love. Some psychologists who study moral judgment argue that our convictions come quickly, from the gut, and our reasons follow to defend them, which would explain why a good argument at the table so rarely changes a mind. Those who say faith should stay out of politics are right that the church isn't a party, and those who say the stakes are moral are right that some of them are.

What these explanations leave out is what the fight is usually about. Beneath a great deal of political anger is fear for something loved: children, a country, a faith or a way of life that seems to be slipping, a vulnerable neighbor no one else will defend. The person across the table is often afraid of losing something too. And beneath the fear is a question of where we've put our hope. When politics carries the weight faith is meant to carry, a family member who votes the other way doesn't feel merely mistaken. They feel like a traitor.

scripture.intro: The Bible was written by people who lived under empires and inside quarreling families, and it doesn't treat politics as small. It also refuses to let a king, a nation, or a cause sit where God sits. We begin with a lament, because Scripture lets you tell God you're tired of the fighting before it asks anything of you.

passages.text: In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me. Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips and a deceitful tongue. ... Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar! Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace. I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war.
passages.reading: This is the first of the psalms headed "A song of ascents" (Psalms 120 to 134). Meshech and Kedar were peoples far from Jerusalem and from each other, so the psalmist seems to be naming the company he keeps rather than his address. He's worn out by lying lips and people who hate peace. You can say the same to God in his words. He leaves the deceitful tongue for God to answer (Psalm 120:3-4), and the songs that follow climb until Psalm 133 sings, "how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!" Whoever prays this psalm prays as the one in favor of peace, so it's worth asking whether the people across the table pray it about us.

passages.text: Then the Pharisees went out and conspired to trap Jesus in His words. They sent their disciples to Him along with the Herodians. ... “Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” ... “Show Me the coin used for the tax.” And they brought Him a denarius. “Whose image is this,” He asked, “and whose inscription?” “Caesar’s,” they answered. So Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”
passages.reading: Matthew sets this in the temple courts in Jesus' last days in Jerusalem. The Herodians seem to have backed Herod's family, which ruled by Rome's leave, while many in the crowd resented the tax as a mark of Rome's rule, so two camps that agreed on little agreed on the trap. Say pay, and Jesus loses the crowd. Say don't, and they could "hand Him over to the rule and authority of the governor" (Luke 20:20). He makes them say whose face is on the coin. He doesn't say what bears God's image, but Genesis does: "So God created man in His own image" (Genesis 1:27). Caesar can have the coin. He can't have you, or your father, or your daughter.

passages.text: This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says to all the exiles who were carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters in marriage, so that they too may have sons and daughters. Multiply there; do not decrease. Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper.”
passages.reading: Jeremiah sent this letter from Jerusalem to the people Nebuchadnezzar had carried off to Babylon (Jeremiah 29:1), while other prophets were promising a quick way home (Jeremiah 28:2-4). Babylon's seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10) meant many who read it would die there, so they were to build, plant, marry, and raise grandchildren. Family life wasn't to wait until the politics came out right. Then the hardest line: seek the good of the city that carried you off, and pray for it. The word translated prosperity is shalom, peace and welfare together. If exiles could pray for Babylon's peace, we can pray for a neighbor who votes the other way.

passages.text: My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.
passages.reading: The letter of James was sent "To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion" (James 1:1), believers scattered and under pressure, and it has hard words for a tongue that blesses God and curses "men, who have been made in God's likeness" (James 3:9). These verses give the order we reverse at the table: listen first, speak later, get angry slowly. Political anger feels righteous because it so often rises on behalf of something good. The letter answers that human anger doesn't produce the righteousness God wants. Winning at dinner won't bring your country the justice you want; listening long enough might let you hear what your father or your daughter is actually afraid of.

whyHard:
It's easy to blame the parties, the news, and the phones that learned what makes us angry, and they've earned some of the blame. None of it explains why a vote can feel like a betrayal from a son or a mother. Families have argued about kings and taxes for as long as there have been kings and taxes. What's new is what we've asked politics to carry.

For most of Western history, faith carried the heaviest things in a life: who you were, where you belonged, what to fear, and what would finally set the world right. As that shared faith has thinned, politics has picked up the load, and it carries it the way a religion would, with a story of salvation, a community of the righteous, and an enemy. Once a party or a cause holds that much of us, the people who vote differently start to look like heretics.

The church has lived both without power and too close to it. An early Christian writing, the Letter to Diognetus, usually dated to the second or third century, described believers who lived in their own countries as sojourners, married and raised children like their neighbors, and passed their days on earth as citizens of heaven. After Constantine turned toward the Christian faith in 312, the church in the West spent more than a thousand years close to the throne, and we inherited a habit of looking to government for what only God and his people can do. When government fails us, the other party starts to look like the enemy of God.

In our country the temptation wears two faces. One conscripts the cross into a flag, until faithfulness to Christ and loyalty to the nation can't be told apart and the nation stands where the Bible puts God's people. The other drafts the gospel into a cause, until the church's message can't be told apart from a movement's platform and the movement stands where the Bible puts the kingdom of God. Each keeps the parts of Christ that bless its side and quietly drops the parts that would cost it. Scripture's word for both is idolatry, and it should be said with grief, because both usually begin in love, for a country or for the vulnerable, which is why they're hard to see from inside. One word for both doesn't make them the same size. In one family the flag is the live danger, in another the cause, and we're quicker to spot the one we don't carry.

I'm a pastor, and I can't write this from outside it. Many of us, pastors included, give more of the week to voices that profit from our fear than to Scripture and prayer, and then wonder why the table sounds more like the feed than like Christ. I came to faith from atheism, so I understand why someone outside the church might hear our politics as one more tribe with a God attached. If you're reading this without faith and you've watched Christians make the fighting worse in God's name, that's a fair charge, and the church should hear it first.

The sociologist James Davison Hunter argued in *To Change the World* (2010) that Christians on the right and the left have shared a quiet assumption, that politics is the main way to change the world, and he proposed instead what he called faithful presence: Christians fully present in their homes, their work, and their towns, seeking the good of the place rather than control of it. It sounds a great deal like Jeremiah's letter, and it starts at your own table. The way through isn't caring less about your country or the people you're afraid for. It's loving them in the right order, with Christ in the place no party can hold, so that the people at your table are family again before they're anything else. You can reorder only your own allegiance, and the temptation will be to start with theirs.

thisWeek.intro: You can't fix your family's politics this week, and it isn't your job to. These steps are small on purpose. If you're afraid of someone at home, use the help lines at the end of this page instead.

steps.title: Pray for them by name
steps.body: Before the next call or family dinner, pray for the person you're most at odds with, by name, and not that they'll change their vote. Pray for their health, their sleep, and the fear under their anger. Jesus told his followers to pray even for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44).

steps.title: Talk about anything else
steps.body: Call, text, or visit with no politics in it. Ask about the grandkids, the garden, or the game, or share a good memory. People need to know you love them for more than their opinions, and they won't learn it in the middle of an argument. One ordinary conversation reminds you both that you were family long before this election.

steps.title: Ask before you answer
steps.body: When politics comes up, ask one real question before you make a point: *What worries you most about it?* Then listen until you can say their view back in words they'd agree with. Proverbs is blunt: "He who answers a matter before he hears it— this is folly and disgrace to him" (Proverbs 18:13). You can understand someone and still disagree.

steps.title: Know when to stop
steps.body: Not every gathering has to be a debate, and you're allowed to say so: *I love you too much to keep doing this tonight.* If you can, agree ahead of time that politics stays off the holiday table. When voices rise, take a walk, and keep children out of the crossfire.

steps.title: Turn down the noise
steps.body: For one day this week, skip the political news and the feeds, and read a psalm instead: Psalm 120, or Psalm 146, which warns, "Put not your trust in princes" (Psalm 146:3). Notice what happens to your sleep and your temper. You can stay informed on far less than you're getting.

steps.title: Pray for the leader you didn't vote for
steps.body: Scripture asks for prayer "for kings and all those in authority" (1 Timothy 2:2), with no exception for the ones you voted against. Pray for them by name, for wisdom and for the good of the people they serve. Then name to God one sin your own side excuses. That part is harder, and it's where contempt starts to lose its grip, because it's hard to look down on anyone right after a confession.

moreHelp.body:
Much family conflict over politics is a pastoral matter that prayer, patience, and honest talk can carry. Some of it isn't. Threats, violence, or a family member who controls who you see, what you spend, or how you vote are safety matters: call 911 if you're in danger, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline, listed with the other help lines at the end of this page, can help you plan. If someone you love talks seriously about hurting people over politics, tell the police, whichever side they're on.

A counselor can help when the conflict has taken over your sleep or your marriage, when you've been cut off from someone you love and the grief isn't easing, or when children are caught in it. A licensed marriage and family therapist can work with the whole family, though not while someone in it is threatening or controlling another; then each person needs help of their own, and safety comes first. Your doctor can refer you, your insurer keeps a directory, and a pastor you trust may know good counselors nearby. Check that anyone you see, Christian or not, is licensed in your state.
signs: Someone at home has threatened, hit, or frightened you. Call 911 if you're in danger now.
A family member controls who you see, what you spend, or how you vote. The Domestic Violence Hotline can help.
Someone you love talks about hurting people over politics as though they mean it. Tell the police.
Children in your home are frightened by the fighting or pulled into it.
Dread or rage about the news has taken over your sleep, appetite, or work for weeks.
An older parent's fear or suspicion has changed suddenly, or comes with confusion. Tell their doctor.
You've had thoughts of ending your life. Call or text 988 now.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need the right words. You can say, *Our family can't talk about politics without it blowing up, and it's hurting us.* If it has turned frightening, say that plainly. Then ask a few questions. Are you licensed in this state? Do you work with families who disagree about things that matter to them? How do you keep your own politics out of the room? How do you handle a client's faith? What does a session cost?
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't keep you from help. Many counselors offer sliding-scale fees, community mental health centers and university training clinics usually charge less, and an employee assistance program through your job may cover a few free sessions. Ask your insurer whether it covers family sessions, since some plans don't. A church you trust may have a benevolence fund.

helping.body:
If you're close to someone whose family is splitting, the first gift is refusing to join the fight against their family, even if you agree with them. Let them grieve. Don't pour your anger on top of theirs, and don't rush them toward a reconciliation they can't make yet. If you're trying to reach a family member swallowed by the news or the feed, ask about their fear before you argue with their facts.

If you lead in a church, you owe a divided congregation the whole Bible preached with no party's thumb on the scale, and your own side's sins named first. Members owe leaders patience: don't demand that a pastor bless your side or condemn the other, and bring a concern to them directly instead of campaigning in the parking lot. Faithful pastors differ on how directly to address public questions from the pulpit. Some believe it must name public sins as the prophets did, or its silence will bless whatever the culture already does; others, that it should preach Christ and leave the application to each conscience, so the cross is never heard as a party's slogan. Either way, the unity you're keeping was given, not negotiated. The letter to the Ephesians asks the church to "preserve the unity of the Spirit" (Ephesians 4:3), a unity it already has in "one Lord, one faith, one baptism" (Ephesians 4:5), and the Lord's Table says the same every time it's set.
say: I love you more than I want to win this.
What worries you most about it?
Help me understand how you see it.
Can we just enjoy dinner tonight?
This doesn't change how much I love you.
You're not wrong to grieve this.
dontSay: How could you vote for that?
No real Christian could believe that.
Your side is ruining this country.
helping.next: After a hard holiday or a blowup, check in a few days later; the hurt often lands after everyone has gone home. Offer to pray with them, or to help them write a short message that doesn't reopen the argument. A church member who feels like a stranger there because of how they vote needs someone to take them for coffee and listen. When a person is afraid of someone at home, ask how it's safe to contact them, since another person may read their phone, and point them to the hotlines at the end of this page. And if anyone talks about not wanting to live, ask plainly whether they're thinking about suicide, and stay with them while they call or text 988.

prayer:
Lord, I'm tired of the fighting. I love people I can hardly talk to anymore, and some of them can hardly stand me. I don't know when an election got this big in my house, but it did, and it got this big in me.

You know what I'm afraid of, and you know what they're afraid of. Give me ears before I open my mouth. Teach me to weep with those who weep, even when they're grieving what I voted for. Keep me from winning an argument and losing a son, a mother, a brother, a friend.

Forgive me for what I've trusted. I've asked a party for what only you can give, and I've let voices on a screen tell me who my enemies are. Remind me that the people across my table bear your image, not a party's.

I'll pray for the leaders I didn't vote for, because you told me to. Help me mean it. Make me more like your Son, who let Caesar have his coin and kept nothing back from you. And keep us at the same table for as long as you give us one. Amen.

faq.q: Should I cut off family over politics?
faq.a: Disagreement alone isn't a reason to end a relationship; families have survived a great deal of it. Contempt and cruelty are another matter, and they may call for firmer limits. You can limit a topic without cutting off a person: *I'd love to see you, and I'm not going to talk about the election.* Paul is honest about limits: "If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone" (Romans 12:18). Your part is only your part. If someone threatens, harms, or controls you, safety comes first, and forgiving them never requires giving them room to hurt you again.

faq.q: My parents watch the news all day. What can I do?
faq.a: Start with what's underneath. A parent who watches all day is often afraid, sometimes lonely, and the television is company that keeps them afraid. Arguing with the channel rarely helps. Ask what worries them most, and listen. Then offer what the news can't: time with you, the grandchildren, a walk, a call about anything but the headlines. If a parent's fear or suspicion has changed suddenly, or comes with confusion, tell their doctor. And it's fair to ask the same question about your own phone.

faq.q: Can a Christian be a Democrat or a Republican?
faq.a: Christians belong to both parties and to neither, and each party asks believers to accept things they have good reason to resist. Many are convinced that one party's stand on a grave question rules it out for them, and some believe it rules it out for every Christian. For one believer it's the protection of unborn life; for another, the treatment of the poor and the stranger. Those convictions usually come from Scripture and a conscience trying to obey it, and believers who weigh the same questions differently owe them respect, not a shrug. You can be sure a brother is wrong about his vote and still call him a brother. What no Christian can give any party is the loyalty that belongs to Christ.

faq.q: Is Christian nationalism the same as patriotism?
faq.a: No. Loving your country and working for its good are right, and Scripture says to "honor the king" (1 Peter 2:17). The label is sometimes thrown at any Christian who loves their country or votes conservative, and that's unfair. Used with care, Christian nationalism names a fusion of faith and nation in which being a faithful Christian and being a loyal American mean the same thing, and the nation takes the place the Bible gives to God's people. Scripture's word for that is idolatry, and the same word fits on the left. Caring about justice is no more the problem than loving your country; the trouble starts when being a faithful Christian and being on the right side of history mean the same thing, and a movement takes the place the Bible gives to the kingdom of God. Either way, the test is whether Christ can still tell you no.

faq.q: Didn't Jesus say he would divide families?
faq.a: He did. Sending out the twelve, Jesus warned, "I have not come to bring peace, but a sword" (Matthew 10:34), and he borrowed words from Micah 7:6: "A man's enemies will be the members of his own household" (Matthew 10:36). In Micah they're a lament over a land where the powerful took bribes and no one could be trusted. In Matthew the division comes from following Jesus: "Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me" (Matthew 10:37). Believers have lost families for confessing Christ, and some still do. That's a cost of loyalty to him, never a license to break with family over a party. Before you claim the verse, ask whether your family is rejecting Jesus or your politics with his name on it.

faq.q: My church is divided over politics. Should I leave?
faq.a: Not over a candidate, if your church still preaches Christ and you can worship there. People who vote differently in one congregation can be a sign of health; Paul wrote that in Christ "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female" (Galatians 3:28), naming the deepest divisions of his world. Talk with your pastor before you decide. Leaving may be wise if the pulpit has traded the gospel for a party's platform, in either direction, and if you've been harmed there, your safety comes before any conversation. If you go, go without slander (telling the truth about harm isn't slander), and don't let one church's failure keep you from finding another.

slots.note: After the paragraph that begins I'm a pastor, which already states his coming to faith from atheism as a stance: if James wants to, a sentence or two in his own words on how Christians' political talk looked to him from outside the church, and what helped him tell Christ apart from a party using his name. The page stands without it.

James is raising five sons. If he wants to, a sentence in his own words on what he hopes his sons learn at his own table about disagreeing with people they love. Nothing about any real conversation unless he tells it.

Where the leaders' part says faithful pastors differ on how directly to address public questions from the pulpit: if James wants to, where he lands as a lead pastor and the founder of the Pastors Connection Network, and how he leads a congregation through an election season, in his own words. The paragraph states both views, each with what it guards, without a landing.

In the answer to Can a Christian be a Democrat or a Republican?: if James wants to, where he lands on whether a conscience can rightly rule out a party, in his own words. The answer gives both convictions room and speaks for no one's vote; nothing about how he votes unless he chooses to say it.
